newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwandan refugees receive cold reception home.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees receive cold reception home.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Rwandan refugees returned home in tattered clothes on Sunday to a cold reception from survivors who remember the dead of the 1994 genocide.
At Nyanza hill, south of the capital Kigali, hundreds of Hutu refugees in small groups walked in silence on a dirt road past rows of 900 wooden crosses to mark a massacre there on April 11, 1994.
From beneath large bundles of belongings perched on their heads, some glanced at the crosses. But many stared straight ahead and ignored the nearby mass grave covered with concrete.

"Though we may forget the massacres, there will be justice," said a sign, which had fallen over on to the red dirt behind the site where Interahamwe militiamen and Hutu troops rounded up Tutsi men, women and children and slaughtered them.

Rwanda's government has appealed for calm during the return from Zaire since November 15 of 600,000 Hutus, many of whom left Rwanda in fear of reprisal attacks for the three-month genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Authorities are registering every returnee but say there will be no arrests of suspects without full investigations.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) says some 15 returnees have been picked up by authorities -- and they were mostly for protective custody to prevent vigilante attacks.
Leaving trails of aid agency biscuit wrappings behind them, thousands of refugees exhausted by weeks on the road walked warily past curious Hutu and Tutsi residents dressed in their Sunday best.

"There shouldn't be any panic in Rwanda. The government is committed to settling the people and then will let justice take its course," said Claude Dusaidi, a senior advisor to military strongman Paul Kagame, who led Tutsi rebels to victory in 1994.

"The Interahamwe have come back to Rwanda and I have seen some of them here but I don't need to take revenge," said Isiah Kayibanda, 44, whose wife and two children were among thousands killed at Nyamata church, 42 km (26 miles) south of Kigali.
Asked what he would do if a former Interahamwe involved in the attack on the packed church in 1994 walked up to him, Kayibanda, a Tutsi farmer, said: "He would make me frightened."

As he spoke workmen dug a deep mass grave in the centre of the church for hundreds of sacks full of bones and skulls piled up at the entrance, from where attackers threw grenades into the building in 1994 to kill those who had sought sanctuary.
"I come here twice a week, every week," said an old man at Ntarama church, where many of the hundreds of dead from 1994 were left to rot where they died as a memorial to the genocide.

"These refugees are no problem of mine -- even if they do include the Interahamwe and Hutu soldiers. I don't care about them. This is my problem, these dead. For genocide survivors this is still a bad dream. We still can't really believe it."
A dusty poster dated March 3, 1994, on the wall above the human remains and belongings still covering the low wooden pews inside the church reads: "Equality, peace and development."
At Sainte Famille Roman Catholic church in Kigali, a Hutu worshipper stepped out of the service and said he was confused by a dispute over the size of the biggest Rwandan refugee exodus from Zaire.

"The national radio says nearly all the refugees who fled in 1994 have returned. But I am a Hutu and have many relatives who went to Zaire and have not come back. Where are they?" he said. "I know they were alive recently so where did they go?"

The government says it agrees with a U.S. military team's assessment that only some 202,000 Rwandan refugees remain in eastern Zaire and include many family members of Interahamwe and former Hutu troops fleeing deeper into the vast country.

But UNHCR says according to its estimates up to more than half a million Hutu refugees remain trapped in eastern Zaire, many short of food and water and are being herded past a swathe of border territory seized by Rwandan-backed Zairean rebels.
